html:
The great movement of Han Chinese into Manchuria from the mid 1800s to the mid 1900s, mostly from Shandong and Hebei. The name means "crashing into Guandong", an old name for Manchuria. Over these decades tens of millions of people moved, and Han Chinese became the great majority of the northeast.

Manchuria was the homeland of the Qing rulers, and for two centuries they kept Han farmers out of most of it. After Russia took the lands north of the Amur and east of the Ussuri in 1858 and 1860, the Qing began opening the region to settlers to hold it.

Migrants came to escape overcrowding, floods and famine, such as the Northern Chinese famine of 1876 to 1879. Many came by sea from Shandong; some went back each winter. They farmed soybeans, cut timber and worked in mines. Railways built by Russia and then Japan, such as the Chinese Eastern Railway, sped the flow.

Japan later took the region and set up the puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932, but the migration went on.
